title: Kenton Cool Summits Everest for 20th Time, Breaking His Own Record and Eyeing More
summary: Kenton Cool isn't ready to hang up his boots. The 52-year-old British mountain guide touched the 8,849-meter summit of Mount Everest for the 20th time on Friday, extending his own record for the most ascents by a non-Sherpa. "Maybe another two or three more times," he told reporters in Kathmandu on Sunday, a striking statement from someone who last year suggested he might climb Everest only once more before shifting to smaller peaks. Cool's milestone came during an extraordinary week on the world's highest mountain. On Wednesday, 274 climbers reached the summit from the Nepali side—a single-day record—after a hazardous serac (a towering, unstable ice block) forced expeditions to delay their attempts and then rush through a narrow window of favorable weather. The bottleneck raised safety concerns. Veteran Sherpa guide Kami Rita, who holds the overall record with more than 30 summits, called for limiting permits. But Cool offered a different solution: focus on climber experience, not raw numbers. "It is the various companies being a little more diligent on who they take," he said, emphasizing that careful scheduling and vetting are more critical than caps. Currently, Nepal requires only a $15,000 permit fee, with no mandatory proof of mountaineering skill. Authorities are drafting new regulations to require demonstrated experience, a move Cool would likely welcome. The 2026 season saw 494 permits issued to foreign climbers, each accompanied by a Sherpa guide, straining the route. Chinese authorities closed the northern approach from Tibet this year, funneling all traffic to Nepal's southern side. Cool's 20th summit cements his legacy among elite high-altitude guides, but his eyes are already on the next climb—proof that for some, the call of the peak never fades.
why_it_matters: Everest has become a symbol of how commercial pressure and record-chasing can clash with safety and ethics in extreme environments. The debate touches on who gets to climb, how regulation should balance income and lives, and what it means when iconic places are pushed to their limit – questions that will only intensify as climate change makes high mountains more dangerous.

background_read: Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and Tibet, is the world's highest peak at 8,849 meters. For decades, it was the ultimate challenge for elite mountaineers, but the rise of commercial guiding in the 1990s turned it into a multimillion-dollar industry. Sherpas, the indigenous people of the Himalayas, are renowned for their high-altitude skills and hold most of the summit records.

Kami Rita, a veteran Sherpa guide, has climbed Everest more than 30 times – the most of any person, Sherpa or non-Sherpa. Kenton Cool’s record is specifically for non-Sherpas, highlighting the deep reliance on Sherpa expertise. Overcrowding has become a serious problem, especially after the 2019 season when long queues in the 'death zone' above 8,000 meters contributed to several deaths.

Nepal’s Department of Tourism earns significant revenue from permit fees, but currently requires no proof of mountaineering experience. The government is now drafting rules to make demonstrated skill mandatory, responding to years of criticism from seasoned climbers who argue that inexperienced clients endanger themselves and others.

China closed its northern route from Tibet this year, forcing all foreign expeditions onto the southern Nepali side and worsening the traffic on a route already under strain. The hazardous serac mentioned in the article is a perennial danger, and its instability this season forced a rushed summit window that broke daily records but raised safety alarms.

perspectives.perspective: Positive – personal achievement and economic value
perspectives.description: Cool’s 20th summit represents extraordinary physical endurance and skill, inspiring future climbers. For Nepal, climbers bring crucial revenue; permit fees and expedition spending support local communities and fund conservation. The record also highlights the mutually dependent partnership between foreign climbers and Sherpas, whose expertise makes such feats possible.

Critics argue that the record-breaking single-day summit, caused by a dangerous rush after a serac delay, is a symptom of a system that prioritizes client summits over safety. Inexperienced climbers, with no mandatory skill checks, can become liabilities. The death zone is unforgiving, and long queues increase exposure to hypothermia, exhaustion, and oxygen depletion.

Everest has shifted from an elite expedition to a commodified experience; this mirrors broader adventure tourism trends worldwide. From a systemic angle, neither permit caps nor vetting alone will solve the problem – improving infrastructure, weather forecasting, and guiding standards are equally important. The closure of the northern route shows how geopolitical decisions can suddenly shift pressure onto one side.

If Nepal enforces mandatory experience rules, the profile of Everest climbers will change, potentially reducing accidents but also limiting access. Climate change is making the Khumbu Icefall more unstable, and warmer temperatures may increase rockfall hazards, which could force route changes or seasonal closures. Cool’s appetite for more ascents suggests that personal record-chasing will continue, putting pressure on authorities to adapt quickly.
